title: A city full of music
hookLine: the city itself stops Hanuman at the gate, and inside, the enemy's capital is full of music and the Vedas

cards: Hanuman, as small as a cat, reaches the gate of Lanka by moonlight. Before he can slip through, a figure steps out of the dark. She is huge and fierce, and she wants to know what a monkey is doing at her gate at night.
Of all the guards in Lanka, she is the one who matters most. She is the city itself.

teach.b: She is Lanka, the city's guardian spirit, called Lankini in many retellings. She blocks his way, mocks him, and strikes him.

teach.h: A CITY FULL OF MUSIC AND VEDAS.
teach.b: Hanuman hits back but holds himself in: Valmiki says he uses only his left fist, not his full force.

Even so, she falls, and from the ground she remembers an old warning from Brahma, the creator: when a monkey overpowers you, the end of the rakshasas has come. Go in, she says. Do what you came to do.
Inside, Valmiki opens the city to us, and it's no cartoon lair. Mansions bright with lamps. Singing and instruments.
And from some houses, the Vedas being chanted. Ravana himself is remembered in the tradition as a great scholar and a devoted worshipper of Shiva.
Lanka is wealthy, beautiful, learned and alive, and somewhere in it a stolen woman sits grieving. That is the hard teaching here.
In Hindu thought, learning, wealth and even prayer don't make a life good. Dharma does: doing what is right toward others.

teach.h: HE KNEW, AND STILL TOOK SITA.
teach.b: Ravana had the Vedas and still took Sita. That's why, at Dussehra, crowds burn the effigy of a scholar-king, not a cartoon monster, and many teachers read his ten heads as the vices that cleverness doesn't cure.
Knowing much and doing right are not the same thing.

how: At Dussehra, many communities burn effigies of Ravana, and storytellers remember him as both a learned devotee of Shiva and the king who would not give Sita back.

o: the monkeys and bears who march with Rama
the gods who watch Hanuman's flight from the sky
the beings of Ravana's city, fierce or graceful

games.q: the gate and the city — tap the pairs.
p: the guardian spirit of the city

s: Valmiki describes Lanka as dark and ugly
he describes it as wealthy, bright, musical and learned.
the city's guardian says her defeat was foretold by Brahma
when a monkey overpowers her, the rakshasas' end is near.
Hindu tradition remembers Ravana as ignorant
he's remembered as a great scholar and Shiva devotee; his fall is about dharma, not brains.

games.q: a friend says Ravana can't be that bad: he chanted the Vedas and worshipped Shiva. what fits today's story?
o: true, someone that learned can't be the villain.
learning and prayer don't make a life good; how you treat others does.
the Vedas in Lanka must have been fake.
games.why: Valmiki shows Lanka learned and musical, and still holding Sita captive. in Hindu thought dharma, doing right, is the test, not knowing much.

practice: Let your attention go to sound, everything you can hear right now, near and far, the many lives of your own city, the way Hanuman hears Lanka. Then, if you pray, ask quietly that what you know this week turns into what you do.
If you don't pray, name one thing you already know is right, and one small way to do it today.

wordCard.voice: Rakshasa, the beings of Ravana's city, whose guardian, Lanka herself, falls to Hanuman's blow and lets him into a capital full of lamps, music and the chanting of the Vedas.

orig.note: Sanskrit rākṣasa, the beings of Ravana's city; rākṣasī for a female.

carryVoice: Your line: learning without dharma still falls. Next, the palace at the city's heart. Day six hundred thirteen, done.
